images.title: File:A view of ruins from Hemakuta Hill, Hampi Karnataka 2.jpg
images.author: Ms Sarah Welch
images.description: Hampi ruins and monuments date to pre-17th century period of South Indian history, particularly those related to the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire era (14th-16th centuries). The site consists of numerous ruins and temples over a large area, the most visited and studied are those located near the Tungabhadra river. The town derives its name from the Pampa Devi Hindu mythology in Sanskrit, with Pampa morphing into Hampa in Kannada, then Hampi. The city served as capital of the Vijayanagara rulers, was pillaged, ruined and abandoned after Muslim armies of a Sultanate coalition attacked and defeated it. In the modern era, it serves as an archaeological site and is a UNESCO world heritage site. The Hemakuta Hill served as a site of few Hindu and Jain temples with a view of other Hampi monuments. It was also a gurukul for artists to learn design and architecture rules for building temples, a practice lab to erect trial temples. The hill has many simple to complex temples, all laid out in square pattern.

images.title: File:A temple water tank, Hampi monuments Karnataka.jpg
images.author: Ms Sarah Welch
images.description: Major temples and associated markets (bazaar) at Hampi featured a water tank. Some are very large, others small. Typical water tanks consisted of a square (or joined squares) stepped well with a central deity shrine and nearby rest mandapa. To some, an aqua duct brought water and drains removed water, while others were below the water table of Tungabhadra river.
